html:
The Great Bengal famine struck the lower Ganges plain in 1769 and 1770, killing millions of people, perhaps a third of the population of Bengal, under the rule of the East India Company.

The rains failed in 1769, and the rice crop with them. Prices soared and people starved through 1770. Disease followed hunger. The Company's own governor, Warren Hastings, later put the dead at about a third of the people; most estimates run to several million, around ten million in some.

Human choices made it worse. Since 1765 the Company had held the right to collect Bengal's land revenue, a reward of its win at Plassey. It kept collecting tax through the famine and even raised the amount taken. Its agents and others were accused of hoarding rice. Little relief was given.

The famine left whole districts empty and helped push Parliament to rein in the Company with the Regulating Act of 1773. It was the first of a series of great famines under British rule, which ran through the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 to the Bengal famine of 1943.
sum: The Great Bengal famine struck the lower Ganges plain in 1769 and 1770, killing millions of people, perhaps a third of the population of Bengal, under the rule of the East India Company.
